title: Fast Radio Bursts
subtitle: A flash in a millisecond
yt_title: A Flash From Space That Lasts 1 Millisecond ⚡ | Ep. 42 #shorts
description:
Episode 42 of a daily journey through the universe. ⚡
Fast radio bursts: flashes of radio waves from far-away galaxies that last about a thousandth of a second, yet release as much energy as the Sun does in days. Some repeat. In 2020 one was traced to a magnetar inside our own galaxy.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 43: Next stop, the Fermi paradox. If the universe is so big, where is everybody?

Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

segments.text: Episode forty-two. Next stop... fast radio bursts.
Imagine a flash that lasts just one thousandth of a second, but carries more energy than the Sun gives out in days.
These are fast radio bursts. The first one was found in two thousand seven, hidden in old data from the Parkes radio telescope in Australia.
segments.headline: First found in 2007

segments.text: Most come from galaxies billions of light-years away. Their light has been travelling since before Earth existed.
segments.headline: From distant galaxies

segments.text: Telescopes now spot them all over the sky. Astronomers think thousands may happen every single day.
Most flash once and disappear. But some repeat, again and again, from the same place.
segments.headline: Some repeat

segments.text: In twenty twenty, a breakthrough. A burst came from inside our own galaxy, from a magnetar, the super-magnetic dead star from episode thirteen.
segments.headline: A clue: a magnetar

segments.text: That magnetar is about thirty thousand light-years away. Close enough to catch it in the act.

visual.label: a burst inside the Milky Way

segments.text: So magnetars make at least some of them. But not all bursts fit, and astronomers are still searching for the rest.
segments.headline: Still a puzzle

segments.text: And because these flashes cross the universe, scientists use them to weigh the gas hidden between galaxies.
segments.headline: Weighing the universe

segments.text: Tomorrow, the biggest question of all. If the universe is so big, where is everybody? Next stop: the Fermi paradox. Follow, so you don't miss episode forty-three.
